title: Research
text:
Vox Populi, Vox Dei: The Rise of the Religious-Conservative Left and the Reconfiguration of Political Space in Latin America.


Abstract


My dissertation examines the unexpected emergence of the Religious Conservative Left in Latin America, analyzing the causes that led to its rise and the factors that have enabled its development. I argue that the Religious Conservative Left is a product of electoral incentives and parties’ organizational constraints. The persistence of religious and culturally conservative values among significant segments of society has created fertile ground for political appeals based on these values. However, electoral incentives alone are insufficient to trigger changes in party platforms. Parties led by autonomous leaders are more capable of adopting these shifts, whereas parties in which activists—particularly culturally progressive groups such as feminists and LGBTQ+ organizations—exercise substantial influence over party decisions and strategies face greater constraints in implementing such changes. Furthermore, the research examines the implications of the Religious Conservative Left for the party system, showing that it has constrained the growth of radical right-wing parties. To assess these claims, I adopt a multi-method approach, examining the cases of MORENA in Mexico and the Workers’ Party (PT) in Brazil.

Peer-Reviewed Publications
Castillo, I., Contreras-Guzmán, D., & Henzi, C. (2023). When do progressive evangelicals mobilize? Intra-denominational competing identities in Chile’s constitutional process. Politics and Religion, 16(2), 301-323.


Abstract


Over the last decade, and throughout the Americas, evangelicals have strongly mobilized in defense of socially conservative agendas or against so-called “gender ideology,” sparking general and academic interest. Much less is known about progressive evangelicals. Using the unique juncture presented by the constitutional process in Chile, we study the politicization of a progressive evangelical identity and ask when these religious groups mobilize. We argue that intra-denominational competition for evangelical identity has played an important role in progressive evangelical mobilization, and more specifically the wish to differentiate themselves from conservative evangelicals, introduce a distance from the political right, and show the internal diversity of the community. This process occurs in response to an initial (conservative) politicization of religion. Drawing on campaign materials, surveys, and interviews, we provide evidence for this argument highlighting that policy preferences and theological interpretations are core differences among both groups, sparking countermobilization.

Working Papers
Contreras-Guzmán, D. The Rise of the Religious Conservative Left in Latin America.


Abstract


This paper explains the surprising emergence of the Religious Conservative Left, a variant of the left that combines left-wing economic policies with culturally conservative and religious platforms. I argue that the persistence of culturally conservative preferences among Latin American voters has created incentives for left-wing parties to adopt Religious Conservatism. However, to do so, the leaders of left-wing parties require high levels of autonomy from their culturally progressive activists. First, an analysis of survey data demonstrates the persistence of cultural conservatism in several Latin American countries. Next, a survey experiment reveals the electoral potential of Religious Conservatism when employed by left-wing candidates. The case of MORENA in Mexico illustrates how left-wing parties with autonomous leadership can embrace Religious Conservatism despite resistance from culturally progressive activists. In contrast, the Workers’ Party in Brazil shows how party organizations that constrain leaders’ autonomy by empowering activists limit the incorporation of new contending groups.


Donoso, S. & Contreras-Guzmán, D. Political Learning and the Rise of Movement Parties: Chile’s Frente Amplio in Comparative Perspective.


Abstract


Amid a broader crisis of political representation, movement parties have emerged as a potential response to the shortcomings of established party systems. Yet the factors shaping their emergence and development remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we focus on the idea of political learning and its importance for movement parties. First, we conceptualize political learning as a critical element for movement parties. Then, we propose three main areas of political learning that are crucial for the development of these parties and their prospects for endurance: their relationship with social movements, their internal organization, and their relationship to mainstream parties within their ideological sector. Using the case of the Chilean Frente Amplio and a multi-method strategy, we show the importance that these learnings have for the formation and trajectories of new movement parties.

title: Danissa Contreras-Guzmán
text:
Welcome! I am a PhD candidate in the Department of Government at the University of Texas at Austin.
My research focuses on the relationship between religion and politics in Latin America. In particular, I examine the incentives and constraints that left-wing parties face when embracing religious and culturally conservative agendas in contemporary politics. I also study the role of religious organizations in state-building processes across the region.
My research has been supported by several organizations, including the APSA Centennial Center, the APSA Religion and Politics Section, the Tinker Foundation, and the Society for the Scientific Study of Religion.
Previously, I received a BA and MA in Political Science from Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile.
